name: data-description
content:
All files are at the root of the competition data.

| File | Size | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `ioai-starter.py` | 8 KB | Working reference solution. Start here. |
| `vocabulary.json` | 16 KB | The 1,602 words. The hidden word is always one of these. |
| `public_embeddings.npy` | 16 MB | `float32`, shape `(1602, 2560)`. Row `i` is the embedding of word `i`. |
| `test_public.json` | 1.5 KB | 120 words for local self-scoring. Disjoint from both hidden rounds. |
| `potato_doc.md` | 13 KB | Beginner-friendly guide to embeddings and cosine similarity. |

## Loading the data

Do not hard-code paths. The grader imports your file from a temporary directory and passes the data location in `POTATO_DATA_DIR`, so a path that works in your notebook will not exist during grading.

`load_public_data()` in `ioai-starter.py` already handles this. Keep its search intact and it returns the vocabulary and the L2-normalized embedding matrix for you.

## The vocabulary

`vocabulary.json` is a JSON list of 1,602 unique lowercase words. Two rules follow from it:

- the hidden word is always in this list;
- **every word you propose must also be in this list.** Proposing anything else fails the round immediately.

Row `i` of `public_embeddings.npy` corresponds to word `i` in `vocabulary.json`. `load_public_data()` returns the matrix L2-normalized, so a dot product between two of its rows is their cosine similarity.

## The splits

| Split | Words | Answers | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|---|
| `test_public` | 120 | provided | local self-scoring |
| `leaderboard-a` | 120 | hidden | Public Leaderboard |
| `leaderboard-b` | 120 | hidden | Private Leaderboard, final ranking |

All three sets are disjoint, and every word in each comes from `vocabulary.json`. There is no training split: nothing is fitted from labelled rows, so `test_public.json` is your only local feedback.

## The private embeddings

Not provided, by design. `public_embeddings.npy` holds *public* embeddings; the judge uses a different, private representation for every comparison.

# OFFICIAL COMPETITION RULES

**ENTRY IN THIS COMPETITION CONSTITUTES YOUR ACCEPTANCE OF THESE OFFICIAL COMPETITION RULES.**

The Competition named below is a skills-based competition intended to promote and further the field of data science and machine learning.

You must register through the Competition Website to enter. To participate, you must agree to these Official Competition Rules, which incorporate by reference the provisions and content of the Competition Website and any Competition-Specific Rules stated below (collectively, the “Rules”).

Please read these Rules carefully before entering the Competition. By entering, participating, or making a Submission, you confirm that you have read, understood, and agreed to these Rules.

These Rules form a binding agreement between each Participant and the Competition Sponsor with respect to the Competition.

All Submissions must comply with the requirements stated on the Competition Website and in these Rules. Submissions will be evaluated using the evaluation metric described on the Competition Website.

This Competition does not offer monetary or non-monetary prizes.

You may not participate in the Competition or make Submissions using more than one Kaggle account.

---

# 1. COMPETITION-SPECIFIC TERMS

## 1.1 Competition Title

IOAI 2026 — Potato Contact

## 1.2 Competition Sponsor

IOAI 2026 - Kazakhstan

## 1.3 Competition Sponsor Address

Kazakhstan, Astana

## 1.4 Competition Website

https://ioai2026.kz/

## 1.5 Prizes

No monetary or non-monetary prizes are offered in this Competition.

## 1.6 Participation Format

The Competition is open to individual Participants and AI Models track Participants only.

Teams, team formation, and team mergers are not permitted.

## 1.7 Submission Format

This is a notebook-based competition.

All valid Submissions must be generated by a Kaggle Notebook associated with the Competition.

Participants must submit through the notebook-based submission workflow specified on the Competition Website.

Direct upload of prediction files or other competition outputs is not permitted.

The submitted notebook must generate the required submission file in the format specified on the Competition Website.

## 1.8 Data and Model Restrictions

Participants may use only:

1. the Competition Data provided by the Competition Sponsor; and
2. permitted software libraries that do not introduce external data or pretrained resources.

The Competition Data includes `public_embeddings.npy`, a pretrained semantic
representation of the vocabulary. Participants may use it freely; it is
Competition Data.

No other pretrained model, model weights, checkpoint, adapter, or embedding may
be used. No external data may be used. Neither the Participant's Kaggle Notebook
nor the graded program has Internet access.

Participants may not attach datasets, models, or other resources that they
created themselves and that are not part of the Competition Data.

The judge evaluates every comparison in a private embedding space that is not
provided. Participants may not attempt to obtain, reconstruct from the grading
environment, or otherwise gain unauthorised access to the private embeddings,
the hidden word lists, or any other grader-side asset.

Solutions are not required to use machine learning. Any legitimate method that solves the task is permitted, including search-based and algorithmic approaches. A solution is not legitimate if it attempts to obtain unauthorised access to validation or test data, or otherwise circumvents the Competition platform.

### Hardware

The Participant's Notebook only writes `submission.csv` and needs no accelerator;
a CPU notebook is sufficient:

- CPU: `"enable_gpu": false` and `"machine_shape": ""`

The graded program is run by the grader on CPU. Requesting a GPU for the Notebook
does not give the graded program a GPU.

---

# 2. COMPETITION-SPECIFIC RULES

In addition to any applicable general Kaggle competition rules, Participants understand and agree to the following Competition-Specific Rules.

## 2.1 Individual Participation

a. Participants must compete individually.

b. Teams are not permitted.

c. Team formation and team mergers are not permitted.

d. A Participant may use only one Kaggle account to enter or participate in the Competition.

e. Sharing private code, private solutions, private predictions, or private competition results between Participants is not permitted.

---

## 2.2 Submission Requirements

a. All valid Submissions must be created and submitted through a Kaggle Notebook associated with the Competition.

b. Direct upload of locally generated prediction files is not permitted.

c. The submitted notebook must generate the required competition output file in the location and format specified on the Competition Website.

d. A Submission may be rejected or disqualified if:

1. it was not generated through the required notebook workflow;
2. it uses prohibited data, models, weights, or external resources;
3. it does not comply with the required submission format;
4. it cannot be reproduced from the submitted notebook and permitted resources; or
5. it otherwise violates these Rules.

e. The submitted notebook must contain the code necessary to reproduce the corresponding Submission.

f. Final submitted notebooks must run with Internet access disabled.

---

## 2.3 Submission Limits

a. A Participant may make a maximum of fifteen (15) scored Submissions to this Competition.

Each `kaggle competitions submit` command creates one Submission and counts towards this limit, whether or not the Submission scores well and whether or not it improves the Participant's standing. Pushing a Kaggle Notebook version with `kaggle kernels push` does not count towards this limit; only Submissions do.

A Notebook version may be submitted to the Competition at most once.

This limit is enforced automatically by the Kaggle platform. Because the Competition runs for a short window, the per-day limit is effectively the total limit.

b. Final Submissions are auto-selected by the system on the basis of Public Leaderboard score. Participants are not required to, and should not, select Final Submissions manually through the Kaggle web interface.

c. All Submission limits are applied individually to each Participant.

d. Each scored round is subject to a grading time limit of six hundred (600)
seconds, i.e. ten (10) minutes. This single budget covers the start-up of the
Participant's program, all preparation and precomputation it performs, and every
game in that round. It is enforced by the grader: a program that exceeds it is
terminated and scores zero for the round.

This limit applies to the grader, not to the Participant's Kaggle Notebook. The
Notebook itself only writes `submission.csv` and is expected to finish in
seconds.

---

## 2.4 Competition Timeline

Competition dates, including the Start Date, Entry Deadline, Final Submission Deadline, and any other applicable deadlines, are shown on the Competition Website under the Competition Timeline.

Participants are responsible for ensuring that all required actions and Submissions are completed before the applicable deadlines.

A Submission counts only if the `kaggle competitions submit` command is sent **before** the Final Submission Deadline. Metric scoring may finish after the deadline; that is permitted. A Submission sent after the deadline is still accepted by Kaggle and still receives a score, but it does not appear on the Leaderboard and does not count towards final ranking.

Participants are advised to submit several minutes before the deadline to allow for platform latency.

---

## 2.5 Competition Data

### a. Permitted Use

Participants may access and use the Competition Data only for:

1. Participating in this Competition;
2. Developing and evaluating solutions for this Competition; and
3. Discussing the Competition on the official Kaggle competition forums.

The Competition Data may not be used for unrelated purposes unless the Competition Sponsor explicitly grants separate permission.

### b. Data Security

Participants must use reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent access to the Competition Data by persons who have not formally agreed to these Rules.

Participants may not transmit, duplicate, publish, redistribute, sell, sublicense, or otherwise make the Competition Data available to any person who is not authorized to access it.

Participants must notify Kaggle and the Competition Sponsor upon becoming aware of any unauthorized access, disclosure, or distribution of the Competition Data.

Participants agree to cooperate in addressing any unauthorized access or distribution.

---

## 2.6 External Data, Models, and Tools

### a. External Data Is Prohibited

Participants may not use any data other than the Competition Data provided by the Competition Sponsor.

Prohibited external data includes, but is not limited to:

1. public datasets;
2. private datasets;
3. purchased datasets;
4. manually collected external data;
5. web-scraped data;
6. data obtained through external APIs;
7. externally sourced labels;
8. external metadata;
9. retrieval databases or external knowledge bases;
10. data generated or enriched using information not included in the Competition Data.

### b. External Pretrained Models Are Prohibited

The pretrained embeddings supplied in the Competition Data
(`public_embeddings.npy`) may be used freely. No *other* pretrained model, model
weights, checkpoint, adapter, or embedding may be used.

Prohibited resources include, but are not limited to:

1. external pretrained models;
2. external model weights;
3. external checkpoints;
4. externally trained adapters;
5. externally trained LoRA weights;
6. external embeddings;
7. external feature representations generated by another pretrained model;
8. external foundation models;
9. external large language models;
10. external vision models;
11. external audio models;
12. external multimodal models.

Participants may not replace, combine, or supplement a prohibited pretrained model
with any external model resource.

### c. Training from scratch

Participants may train models from scratch using only the Competition Data.
Learned parameters created during the notebook run may be used by that run, but
they may not be imported from outside the Competition resources.

### d. External AI Services and APIs

Participants may not use external AI services or APIs to generate:

1. predictions;
2. labels;
3. features;
4. embeddings;
5. training data;
6. validation data;
7. synthetic competition data; or
8. other information used by the submitted solution.

This includes external hosted model APIs and inference services.

### e. Software Libraries

Participants may use generally available software libraries and programming tools, provided that those tools do not introduce prohibited external data, pretrained models, weights, checkpoints, or other restricted resources.

A software package that automatically downloads or includes a pretrained model may not be used unless that model is the specific pretrained model provided by the Competition Sponsor.

---

## 2.7 Internet Access

a. Final submitted notebooks must run with Internet access disabled.

b. A submitted notebook may not download data, model weights, checkpoints, packages containing prohibited pretrained resources, or other external information during execution.

c. All resources required by the final Submission must be included among the Competition resources or otherwise explicitly approved by the Competition Sponsor.

d. Use of Internet access to bypass the Competition’s restrictions on external data or external models is prohibited.

---

## 2.8 Automated Machine Learning Tools

Automated machine learning tools may be used only if they fully comply with all Competition restrictions. This includes only using libraries on the allowed list.

In particular, an automated machine learning tool must not:

1. access external data;
2. use external pretrained models;
3. download external model weights;
4. call external AI APIs;
5. introduce external features or embeddings; or
6. otherwise use resources prohibited by these Rules.

The Participant remains fully responsible for ensuring that every component used by the tool complies with these Rules.

---

## 2.9 Eligibility

Unless otherwise stated on the Competition Website or prohibited by applicable internal policies, employees, interns, contractors, officers, and directors of the Competition Sponsor, Kaggle, and their respective parent companies, subsidiaries, and affiliates may participate.

The Competition Sponsor may determine that certain individuals are not eligible for official ranking or recognition where participation would create a conflict of interest.

All Participants are responsible for complying with applicable laws, regulations, employer policies, and institutional policies.

---

## 2.10 Final Ranking and Reproducibility

a. Final rankings will be determined according to the evaluation metric and final-submission procedure described on the Competition Website.

b. The Competition Organizers may review a top-ranked Participant’s submitted notebook to confirm compliance with these Rules.

c. A top-ranked Participant may be required to provide:

1. the final submitted notebook;
2. training code;
3. inference code;
4. configuration files;
5. dependency information;
6. a description of the computational environment;
7. a description of the methodology;
8. preprocessing details;
9. training details;
10. hyperparameters; and
11. any other information reasonably necessary to reproduce the Submission.

d. The submitted solution must be reproducible using only:

1. the Competition Data;
2. permitted software libraries; and
3. the code and resources included in or permitted for the submitted notebook.

e. A Participant may be disqualified from the final ranking if:

1. the Submission cannot be reproduced;
2. prohibited external data was used;
3. a prohibited pretrained model or external model resource was used;
4. the submitted notebook does not generate the claimed Submission;
5. the Participant refuses to provide reasonably required reproducibility information; or
6. the Participant otherwise violates these Rules.
7. This list is not exhaustive.

f. If a Participant is disqualified, the Competition Sponsor may adjust the final rankings accordingly.

---

## 2.11 No Prizes or Compensation

a. This Competition does not offer monetary prizes.

b. This Competition does not offer non-monetary prizes.

c. Participation does not create any right to payment, compensation, employment, contract work, reimbursement, or other financial benefit.

d. Participants are responsible for their own costs associated with participating in the Competition.

---

## 2.12 Intellectual Property

a. Except for rights expressly granted under these Rules or the Kaggle platform terms, Participants retain ownership of their original code and other original materials created for the Competition.

b. Participants remain responsible for ensuring that they have the right to use any software libraries or other permitted resources included in their Submission.

c. Participants may not include material in a Submission if its license or terms of use prevent the Participant from complying with these Rules.

d. Nothing in these Rules grants a Participant ownership of:

1. the Competition Data;
2. other materials supplied by the Competition Sponsor.

e. Any additional licensing requirements for submitted solutions must be stated separately and clearly on the Competition Website.

---

## 2.13 Compliance Review

The Competition Sponsor may review any Submission for compliance with these Rules.

The Competition Sponsor may request reasonable evidence showing:

1. how the Submission was created;
2. what data was used;
3. what model or models were used;
4. what software dependencies were used;
5. how any models or embeddings were used; and
6. whether the submitted notebook reproduces the Submission.

Failure to provide sufficient information may result in disqualification.

---

## 2.14 Governing Law

Unless otherwise stated in the Competition-Specific Rules, claims arising out of or relating to these Rules will be governed by California law, excluding its conflict-of-laws rules, and will be litigated exclusively in the federal or state courts of Santa Clara County, California, USA.

The parties consent to personal jurisdiction in those courts.

If any provision of these Rules is held to be invalid or unenforceable, all remaining provisions will remain in full force and effect.

---

# 3. KEY DEFINITIONS

For purposes of these Rules:

**Competition Data** means all data officially provided by the Competition Sponsor for use in the Competition.

**Competition Sponsor** means the organization or individual identified in Section 1.2.

**External Data** means any data or information not included in the Competition Data.

**Participant** means an individual registered to participate in the Competition.

**Submission** means a competition entry generated and submitted through the required Kaggle Notebook workflow.

**Submitted Notebook** means the Kaggle Notebook version used to generate a Submission.

**Competition Website** means the official Kaggle competition page identified in Section 1.4.

If you provide any false information relating to the Competition concerning your identity, residency, mailing address, telephone number, email address, ownership of right, or information required for entering the Competition, you may be immediately disqualified from the Competition. ####2. SPONSOR AND HOSTING PLATFORM a. The Competition is sponsored by Competition Sponsor named above. The Competition is hosted on behalf of Competition Sponsor by Kaggle Inc. ("Kaggle"). As a Kaggle.com account holder and user of the Kaggle competition platform, remember you have accepted and are subject to the Kaggle Terms of Service at [www.kaggle.com/terms][2] in addition to these Rules. ####3. COMPETITION PERIOD a. For the purposes of Prizes, the Competition will run from the Start Date and time to the Final Submission Deadline (such duration the “Competition Period”). The Competition Timeline is subject to change, and Competition Sponsor may introduce additional hurdle deadlines during the Competition Period. Any updated or additional deadlines will be publicized on the Competition Website. It is your responsibility to check the Competition Website regularly to stay informed of any deadline changes. YOU ARE RESPONSIBLE FOR DETERMINING THE CORRESPONDING TIME ZONE IN YOUR LOCATION. ####4. COMPETITION ENTRY a. NO PURCHASE NECESSARY TO ENTER OR WIN. To enter the Competition, you must register on the Competition Website prior to the Entry Deadline, and follow the instructions for developing and entering your Submission through the Competition Website. Your Submissions must be made in the manner and format, and in compliance with all other requirements, stated on the Competition Website (the "Requirements"). Submissions must be received before any Submission deadlines stated on the Competition Website. Submissions not received by the stated deadlines will not be eligible to receive a Prize. b. Submissions may not use or incorporate information from hand labeling or human prediction of the validation dataset or test data records. c. If the Competition is a multi-stage competition with temporally separate training and/or test data, one or more valid Submissions may be required during each Competition stage in the manner described on the Competition Website in order for the Submissions to be Prize eligible. d. Submissions are void if they are in whole or part illegible, incomplete, damaged, altered, counterfeit, obtained through fraud, or late. Competition Sponsor reserves the right to disqualify any entrant who does not follow these Rules, including making a Submission that does not meet the Requirements. ####5. INDIVIDUALS AND TEAMS a. Individual Account. You may make Submissions only under one, unique Kaggle.com account. You will be disqualified if you make Submissions through more than one Kaggle account, or attempt to falsify an account to act as your proxy. You may submit up to the maximum number of Submissions per day as specified on the Competition Website. b. Teams. If permitted under the Competition Website guidelines, multiple individuals may collaborate as a Team; however, you may join or form only one Team. Each Team member must be a single individual with a separate Kaggle account. You must register individually for the Competition before joining a Team. You must confirm your Team membership to make it official by responding to the Team notification message sent to your Kaggle account. Team membership may not exceed the Maximum Team Size stated on the Competition Website. c. Team Merger. Teams may request to merge via the Competition Website. Team mergers may be allowed provided that: (i) the combined Team does not exceed the Maximum Team Size; (ii) the number of Submissions made by the merging Teams does not exceed the number of Submissions permissible for one Team at the date of the merger request; (iii) the merger is completed before the earlier of: any merger deadline or the Competition deadline; and (iv) the proposed combined Team otherwise meets all the requirements of these Rules. d. Private Sharing. No private sharing outside of Teams. Privately sharing code or data outside of Teams is not permitted. It's okay to share code if made available to all Participants on the forums. ####6. SUBMISSION CODE REQUIREMENTS a. Private Code Sharing. Unless otherwise specifically permitted under the Competition Website or Competition Specific Rules above, during the Competition Period, you are not allowed to privately share source or executable code developed in connection with or based upon the Competition Data or other source or executable code relevant to the Competition (“Competition Code”). This prohibition includes sharing Competition Code between separate Teams, unless a Team merger occurs. Any such sharing of Competition Code is a breach of these Competition Rules and may result in disqualification. b. Public Code Sharing. You are permitted to publicly share Competition Code, provided that such public sharing does not violate the intellectual property rights of any third party. If you do choose to share Competition Code or other such code, you are required to share it on Kaggle.com on the discussion forum or notebooks associated specifically with the Competition for the benefit of all competitors. By so sharing, you are deemed to have licensed the shared code under an Open Source Initiative-approved license (see [www.opensource.org][3]) that in no event limits commercial use of such Competition Code or model containing or depending on such Competition Code. c. DETERMINING WINNERS a. Each Submission will be scored and ranked by the evaluation metric stated on the Competition Website. During the Competition Period, the current ranking will be visible on the Competition Website's Public Leaderboard. The potential winner(s) are determined solely by the leaderboard ranking on the Private Leaderboard, subject to compliance with these Rules. The Public Leaderboard will be based on the public test set and the Private Leaderboard will be based on the private test set. b. In the event of a tie, the Submission that was entered first to the Competition will be the winner. In the event a potential winner is disqualified for any reason, the Submission that received the next highest score rank will be chosen as the potential winner. ####8. NOTIFICATION OF WINNERS & DISQUALIFICATION a. The potential winner(s) will be notified by email. b. If a potential winner (i) does not respond to the notification attempt within one (1) week from the first notification attempt or (ii) notifies Kaggle within one week after the Final Submission Deadline that the potential winner does not want to be nominated as a winner or does not want to receive a Prize, then, in each case (i) and (ii) such potential winner will not receive any Prize, and an alternate potential winner will be selected from among all eligible entries received based on the Competition’s judging criteria. c. In case (i) and (ii) above Kaggle may disqualify the Participant. However, in case (ii) above, if requested by Kaggle, such potential winner may provide code and documentation to verify the Participant’s compliance with these Rules. If the potential winner provides code and documentation to the satisfaction of Kaggle, the Participant will not be disqualified pursuant to this paragraph. d. If a Participant is removed from the Competition Leaderboard, additional winning features associated with the Kaggle competition platform, for example Kaggle points or medals, may also not be awarded. f. The final leaderboard list will be publicly displayed at Kaggle.com. Determinations of Competition Sponsor are final and binding. ####9. PRIZES a. Prize(s) are as described on the Competition Website and are only available for winning during the time period described on the Competition Website. The odds of winning any Prize depends on the number of eligible Submissions received during the Competition Period and the skill of the Participants. b. All Prizes are subject to Competition Sponsor's review and verification of the Participant’s eligibility and compliance with these Rules, and the compliance of the winning Submissions with the Submissions Requirements. In the event that the Submission demonstrates non-compliance with these Competition Rules, Competition Sponsor may at its discretion take either of the following actions: (i) disqualify the Submission(s); or (ii) require the potential winner to remediate within one week after notice all issues identified in the Submission(s) (including, without limitation, the resolution of license conflicts, the fulfillment of all obligations required by software licenses, and the removal of any software that violates the software restrictions). c. Prize(s) will be awarded within approximately thirty (30) days after receipt by Competition Sponsor or Kaggle of the required Prize acceptance documents. Transfer or assignment of a Prize is not allowed. e. You are not eligible to receive any Prize if you do not meet the Eligibility requirements in Section 2.7 and Section 3.1 above. f. If a Team wins a monetary Prize, the Prize money will be allocated in even shares between the eligible Team members, unless the Team unanimously opts for a different Prize split and notifies Kaggle before Prizes are issued. ####10. TAXES a. ALL TAXES IMPOSED ON PRIZES ARE THE SOLE RESPONSIBILITY OF THE WINNERS. Payments to potential winners are subject to the express requirement that they submit all documentation requested by Competition Sponsor or Kaggle for compliance with applicable state, federal, local and foreign (including provincial) tax reporting and withholding requirements. Prizes will be net of any taxes that Competition Sponsor is required by law to withhold. As a Kaggle.com account holder, you have the right to request access to, review, rectification, portability or deletion of any personal data held by Kaggle about you by logging into your account and/or contacting Kaggle Support at <[www.kaggle.com/contact][7]>. b. name: Description
content:
## The task

Your friend suggests playing a guessing game. He, as the judge, picks one hidden word from a fixed vocabulary of 1,602 words, and **you must find it in at most 30 turns.**

Each turn the judge compares two words and reports which is semantically closer to the hidden word. Every game starts from the fixed pair `lamp vs potato`, because they are two of your friend's favorite things. Your program then proposes one new word. The winner of the comparison is kept and compared against your next proposal.

You win a game the moment you propose the hidden word exactly. Matching is case-insensitive. Every word you propose must be in `vocabulary.json`.

## The catch

You are given `public_embeddings.npy`, a semantic representation of every word in the vocabulary. These are *public* embeddings; **the judge uses a different, private representation.**

You can self-score locally against the public embeddings, but that judge is not the official one. A local score is only a guide, never a prediction of your leaderboard position.

## What you submit

There is a full example in `ioai-starter.py` with the grader contract and data loading. You can change the `PotatoPlayer` class.

This is a Kaggle code competition, but an unusual one: your notebook does not predict anything. It base64-encodes your solution source into `submission.csv`. The grader then decodes that source, **imports it as a Python module**, and plays every hidden game by calling your `PotatoPlayer` directly. Your program is initialized once per leaderboard round and plays every game in that round, with `new_game()` called between games.

See the **Evaluation** tab for the exact contract. Run `python ioai-starter.py` locally first: it checks that the grader can use your file, and self-scores it.

## Where to find everything

| Topic | Tab |
|---|---|
| Files, vocabulary, embeddings, splits | **Data** |
| The grader contract, `submission.csv` format, and the metric | **Evaluation** |
| Submission flow, limits, and hard rules | **Kaggle CLI Submission** |
| Starting and continuing your agent | **Starter Prompt** / **Continuation Prompt** |
| The technical report you must write | **Report Generation Prompt** |

name: Scoring
content:
## The Judge

The grader **imports your submitted file as a Python module** and calls your objects directly. It does not run your file as a program, so there is no stdin/stdout protocol and your `if __name__ == "__main__":` block never executes during grading.

Your file must define exactly two names:

```python
def load_public_data():
    """Return (words, embeddings): list[str] of length 1602, and a
    (1602, 2560) float32 numpy array whose row i is the embedding of words[i]."""

class PotatoPlayer:
    def __init__(self, words, embeddings): ...   # exactly two arguments
    def new_game(self): ...                      # reset per-game state
    def respond(self, message): ...              # RETURN one vocabulary word
```

Both names are looked up by exact spelling. Renaming either, or giving `__init__` a different number of parameters, fails every game in the round.

Your program is initialized once per leaderboard round and plays every game in that round; the grader calls `new_game()` before each game to reset per-game state.

A worked example, with the hidden word shown only to explain the contract:

```text
Hidden word: shovel          Fixed opening: lamp vs potato

-> respond({"turn": 1, "winner_word": "potato", "verdict": "second", "word1": "lamp",   "word2": "potato"})
<- returns "rock"
-> respond({"turn": 2, "winner_word": "rock",   "verdict": "second", "word1": "potato", "word2": "rock"})
<- returns "hammer"
-> respond({"turn": 3, "winner_word": "hammer", "verdict": "second", "word1": "rock",   "word2": "hammer"})
<- returns "shovel"                                          <- matches: game won
```

Turns are indexed from 1 to 30.

The `verdict` options are `first` meaning that word1 is closer, `second` meaning that word2 is closer, or `same` meaning that both words are equally close to the hidden word.

`winner_word` is the word retained for the next comparison. On a `same` verdict, the first word stays.

`respond()` receives a plain Python dict, already parsed, and must **return** the proposed word as a plain string. Do not print it and do not wrap it in JSON: the grader ignores standard output, so `print()` is harmless but invisible.

## Metric

A game found on turn `t` scores `1.0 - 0.02 x max(0, t - 10)`; a game not solved within 30 turns scores `0`. So turns 1-10 score `1.00`, turn 20 scores `0.80`, turn 30 scores `0.60`.

Your round score is the mean game score x 100, between `0.00` and `100.00`. Higher is better.

The 600-second limit is a single budget covering start-up, preparation and all 120 games in the round.

A failure is terminal for the round: a return value that is not a vocabulary word, a missing or misnamed `load_public_data` / `PotatoPlayer`, or any exception raised from `__init__`, `new_game()`, or `respond()` fails the current game **and every remaining game** in that round.

## Submission format

`submission.csv` must have exactly two columns and two rows:

```csv
id,program_b64
leaderboard-a,<base64 of your solution source>
leaderboard-b,<base64 of your solution source>
```

**Both rows carry the same payload.** Kaggle scores the Public Leaderboard from the `leaderboard-a` row and the Private Leaderboard from `leaderboard-b`. A submission whose rows disagree is rejected.

`ioai-starter.py` writes this file for you when it runs on Kaggle.

## Check your interface before you submit

`kaggle kernels push` only runs the base64 envelope, so a kernel reports `COMPLETE` **even if your interface is wrong**. The import-based grading happens only on `kaggle competitions submit`, and that spends one of your 15.

Check it locally first:

```bash
python ioai-starter.py
```

It verifies the contract and self-scores against the public embeddings. The starter runs the same check inside your Kaggle kernel, so an interface mistake fails the push instead of costing a submission.

name: Kaggle CLI Submission
content:
This competition is **notebook-only**: predictions cannot be uploaded as a submissions.csv file (and even if it can, these will be invalid).
Every submission must come from a notebook that ran on Kaggle's servers. The
steps below do that entirely from the command line.

## Limits for this competition

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Scored submissions | **15 total** (per Participant) |
| Grader time limit | **600 seconds (10 minutes)** for all 120 games in a round |
| Solution source size | 512 KB |
| Concurrent CPU sessions | 5 |
| Concurrent GPU sessions | 2 |
| Internet in the notebook | Disabled |
| Team size | 1 |

### The 600-second limit is the grader's, not your kernel's

There are two different programs in this competition, and they have nothing to
do with each other:

- **Your Kaggle kernel** only base64-encodes your source into `submission.csv`
  and finishes in a couple of seconds. It does not train, predict, or play
  games, and it needs no GPU. Do not pass `--timeout`; the default is plenty.
- **The grader program** is what actually plays the 120 hidden games. It is
  allowed 600 seconds in total, covering its start-up, all precomputation, and
  every game in the round. A program that exceeds it is stopped and scores zero
  for the round. You control this budget by how much work your `PotatoPlayer`
  does, not by any Kaggle flag.

These are two different environments, so a library that imports fine in your
kernel is not guaranteed to exist where your code is graded. Assume the Python
standard library plus NumPy, which is what the starter uses.

## The deadline rule

`kaggle competitions submit` must be **sent before the competition deadline**.

- Submit before the deadline, scoring finishes after it: **counts**.
- Notebook finished in time but you submit after the deadline: does not count.
- Notebook still running at the deadline: does not count.

Late submissions are still accepted and still produce a score you can see, but
they never appear on the leaderboard. Grading 120 games is not instant, so aim
to submit a few minutes early.

## Report requirement

The `.py` file you submit should carry a short technical report in a comment
block at the very top. See the **"Report Generation Prompt"** tab for the
template. The report carries no score.

## Before you start

Accept the competition rules in your browser. There is no CLI equivalent:

```
https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/<competition-slug>/rules
```

Then install and authenticate the CLI:

```bash
pip install kaggle
export KAGGLE_API_TOKEN="KGAT_..."   # from kaggle.com -> Settings -> API
```

## Step 1: Create the notebook folder

A notebook is a folder holding exactly two files:

```
my-solution/
├── script.py
└── kernel-metadata.json
```

## Step 2: Attach the data in `kernel-metadata.json`

Your notebook has **no internet access**. Potato needs no GPU and no extra
datasets — only the competition data itself:

```json
{
  "id": "<your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug>",
  "title": "My Solution",
  "code_file": "script.py",
  "language": "python",
  "kernel_type": "script",
  "is_private": true,
  "enable_gpu": false,
  "enable_internet": false,
  "machine_shape": "",
  "dataset_sources": [],
  "competition_sources": ["<competition-slug>"],
  "kernel_sources": [],
  "model_sources": []
}
```

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| `competition_sources` | Mounts the vocabulary, public embeddings, `test_public.json`, and `ioai-starter.py` |
| `enable_internet` | Must stay `false` |
| `enable_gpu` | Leave `false`; the kernel only writes a CSV |

`dataset_sources` is empty on purpose: everything you need is in the
competition data. Do not attach external datasets or models.

## Step 3: Write `script.py`

Start from the official starter, `ioai-starter.py` (it is in the competition
data). It is a complete working solution that already implements both halves of
this task. **Keep its `load_public_data()`, its contract check, and its Kaggle
block unchanged; edit only the body of the `PotatoPlayer` class.**

The same file is used in two different ways:

- On Kaggle, `/kaggle/working` exists, so its `__main__` block base64-encodes the
  whole file into `submission.csv`. That is all the kernel does.
- Inside the grader, the file is **imported as a Python module**. Its `__main__`
  block never runs. The grader calls your objects by name instead:

```python
words, embeddings = load_public_data()     # once per round
player = PotatoPlayer(words, embeddings)   # once per round
player.new_game()                          # before each of the 120 games
new_word = player.respond(message)         # each turn; RETURNS a str
```

There is no stdin, no stdout protocol, and no JSON on the wire. `respond()`
receives a plain dict and must **return** a vocabulary word. See the
**"Evaluation"** tab for the full contract.

When it runs on Kaggle it writes:

```csv
id,program_b64
leaderboard-a,<base64 of this file>
leaderboard-b,<base64 of this file>
```

Four rules that cause most first-time failures:

- `submission.csv` must have the exact header `id,program_b64` and **exactly
  two rows**, `leaderboard-a` and `leaderboard-b`, carrying the **same**
  base64 payload. Rows that disagree are rejected.
- Keep the names `load_public_data` and `PotatoPlayer` exactly as spelled, and
  keep `__init__(self, words, embeddings)` at exactly two arguments. The grader
  looks these up by name; renaming either fails every game in the round.
- `respond()` must **return** a word from `vocabulary.json`. Returning anything
  else, or printing instead of returning, fails the round.
- Do not change the part of the starter that detects `/kaggle/working`, or the
  `check_contract()` call. That check is what turns an interface mistake into a
  failed push rather than a wasted submission.

### A kernel that says COMPLETE does not mean your interface is right

`kaggle kernels push` runs only the base64 envelope, so it succeeds regardless
of what your `PotatoPlayer` looks like. The import-based grading happens only on
`kaggle competitions submit`, and it costs one of your 15.

Run `python script.py` locally before every submission. It checks the grader
contract and self-scores. The starter runs the same check inside your kernel, so
a renamed class or wrong `__init__` signature stops the push instead of burning
a submission.

## Step 4: Run the notebook on Kaggle

```bash
kaggle kernels push -p my-solution/
```

If the first push after newly attaching `competition_sources` fails with
`FileNotFoundError`, the data mount was not ready yet. Pushing again resolves
it. The retry does not cost a submission — only submissions are counted.

Each push prints a version number. Record it — you need it to submit:

```
Kernel version 3 successfully pushed.
```

Then wait for the run to finish:

```bash
kaggle kernels status <your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug>
```

Statuses go `QUEUED -> RUNNING -> COMPLETE` (or `ERROR`). Poll every
~15 seconds. A potato kernel is fast; it should complete in well under a
minute.

Concurrency limits apply across all your notebooks at once: **5** CPU sessions,
**2** GPU sessions. Exceeding them rejects the push with
`Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached`.

## Step 5: Check the output (optional but recommended)

```bash
kaggle kernels output <your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug> -p out/
```

This downloads `submission.csv` and the run log. Verify it has the
`id,program_b64` header and two rows before spending a submission.

## Step 6: Submit

```bash
kaggle competitions submit <competition-slug> \
  -k <your-kaggle-username>/<your-notebook-slug> \
  -v <version-number> \
  -f submission.csv \
  -m "short description"
```

`-f submission.csv` is **not** a local file path. It names an output file that
already exists in the completed notebook version on Kaggle. Nothing is uploaded
from your machine.

Submitting does **not** re-run your kernel. It hands the encoded source from
that version to the grader, which plays the 120 hidden games. This is why a
potato submission takes longer to score than an ordinary metric: real gameplay
happens at scoring time.

## Step 7: Read your score

```bash
kaggle competitions leaderboard <competition-slug> --show
kaggle competitions submissions <competition-slug>
```

## Self-scoring before you submit

`test_public.json` holds 120 words with answers, disjoint from both hidden
rounds. Running `python script.py` on your machine drives your `PotatoPlayer`
through exactly the call sequence the grader uses, judged with the public
embeddings. Use it to iterate quickly and to catch interface and crash errors
before spending a submission.

Treat that number as an upper bound, not a prediction. Because the judge uses a
different embedding space, self-judged scores run far higher than leaderboard
scores, and a change that helps locally may not help on the leaderboard.

## Submission limits

**Your budget is 15 scored submissions.**

Every `kaggle competitions submit` spends one of the 15, whether or not the
score improves. Pushing a new kernel version is free and does not count — you
may push as many times as you need. Only submissions are limited.

### `submission-limits` tracks this budget

Unlike a notebook-version budget, this one is a real submission count, so
`kaggle competitions submission-limits <competition-slug>` is the correct way
to check it:

```bash
kaggle competitions submission-limits <competition-slug>
# Submissions today: 3
# Remaining today: 12
```

The competition runs for a short window, so the daily limit is effectively your
total limit. Kaggle enforces it.

Practical consequences:

- Do not submit speculatively. A submission that scores 0 still spends one of
  your 15.
- Validate before submitting: self-score on `test_public.json`, confirm the CSV
  header is `id,program_b64`, and confirm both rows carry the same payload.
- Kaggle occasionally starts a run before the competition data has finished
  mounting, which fails with `FileNotFoundError`. This is intermittent platform
  behaviour and cannot be prevented from your side. Pushing again resolves it,
  and costs nothing because pushes are free.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
|---|---|
| `FileNotFoundError` on the first push after attaching the competition | The data mount was not ready. Pushing again resolves it; it does not spend a submission. |
| Submission rejected: rows disagree | `submission.csv` has two different `program_b64` payloads. Both rows must carry the same base64 source. |
| Round scores 0 | A return value outside `vocabulary.json`, or a crash, is terminal: it fails the current game **and every remaining game** in that round. Run `python script.py` locally first. |
| `PotatoPlayer.__init__() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given` | Your `__init__` does not accept `(self, words, embeddings)`. The grader always passes both positionally. |
| `the submitted solution does not define load_public_data()` | You renamed or removed `load_public_data`. The grader looks it up by exact spelling. |
| Kernel says `COMPLETE` but the submission errors | Expected if your interface is wrong: the kernel only runs the base64 envelope. Run `python script.py` locally to check the contract. |
| `Maximum batch GPU session count of 2 reached` | Wait for a running GPU session to finish, or use a CPU notebook (potato needs none). |
| Submission accepted but absent from the leaderboard | It was sent after the deadline. Submit earlier next time. |
| Leaderboard score is far below your self-judged score | Expected: the judge uses a private embedding space. The gap is the task. |
| `submission.csv` has more or fewer than 2 rows | It must contain exactly `leaderboard-a` and `leaderboard-b`. |

name: Report Generation Prompt
content:
Every submitted solution should carry a short technical report describing **the solution in that file**.

## What the report is for

- It carries **no score**. It does not affect your Public or Private Leaderboard position.
- It is a reference for your team and for the IOAI Jury if you need to appeal a score, since agent-written code can be hard to read.
- After the contest and after your redaction, the report is published alongside your de-anonymised score on the final leaderboard, for transparency.

## Where it goes

Inside a comment block at the **very top** of the solution file you submit, above the imports.

## Length and focus

8-10 short paragraphs. Describe the **submitted solution to this task**, not your agentic system, harness, or prompting strategy.

## Prompt

Use this prompt to generate or refresh the report:

```
Write the technical report for the solution you are about to submit. Place it as
a comment block at the very top of the file, above the imports.

Write 8-10 short paragraphs. Describe only the submitted solution: what it does,
why, and what you measured. Do not describe your agent, harness, or prompting
strategy. Be specific and quantitative wherever you can.

Cover at least:
```
